common_name: Pocahontas Possumhaw Holly (Red-Fruited Female Deciduous Holly)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in spring or fall in moist to average, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Pocahontas is a female selection and needs a male Ilex decidua such as 'Red Escort' within pollinating range to set fruit.

directions: Pocahontas is a long-grown female selection of possumhaw holly valued for a heavy, reliable set of glossy red berries that line the bare gray stems after the leaves drop in fall, holding their color deep into winter and drawing mockingbirds and migrating robins. Its upright, multi-stemmed habit and relatively quick growth make it useful as a large informal screen or specimen at a woodland edge, where its winter silhouette becomes a focal point once the surrounding canopy is bare. Like other possumhaw selections it tolerates both moist bottomland soils and drier upland sites, and it responds well to occasional thinning of crowded interior stems to keep the berry-laden branches visible. Underplant with evergreen shrubs or groundcovers so the winter fruit display reads clearly against a darker backdrop.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension — Ilex decidua Plant Profile

common_name: Red Cascade Possumhaw Holly (Pale-Bark Weeping-Branched Deciduous Holly)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist to average, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Red Cascade is a female selection and needs a male Ilex decidua nearby for reliable berry set.

directions: Red Cascade stands out among possumhaw selections for its noticeably pale, almost silvery bark and horizontal, gently spreading branch structure, which gives the winter silhouette a looser, more weeping character than the stiffly upright habit of cultivars like Warren's Red. The bright red berries that form after leaf drop stand out sharply against the light-colored stems, extending the ornamental season well into winter and feeding overwintering songbirds. It adapts to the same range of moist bottomland and drier upland soils typical of the species, making it a flexible choice for naturalistic plantings along a woodland margin or stream edge where its arching branches have room to spread. Prune minimally and only to remove crossing or damaged wood, since the open, spreading form is part of its appeal.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension — Ilex decidua Plant Profile

common_name: Sentry Possumhaw Holly (Narrow Columnar Deciduous Holly)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist to average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Sentry is a female selection prized for its narrow columnar form in tight spaces and needs a male Ilex decidua nearby to set fruit.

directions: Sentry was selected for a distinctly narrow, upright, columnar habit that sets it apart from the broader, spreading form typical of most possumhaw hollies, reaching a full 20 feet in height while staying tight enough in width to fit along a driveway, fence line, or narrow side yard where a standard possumhaw would quickly overrun the space. Its leaves drop earlier in fall than many cultivars, revealing the red berry-studded stems sooner and extending the length of the winter display. As with all possumhaw selections, berries form only on female plants, so a male pollinator growing within range is necessary for a full fruit set. Its tight profile also makes it useful in a repeated row planting as an informal narrow screen along a woodland garden boundary.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension — Ilex decidua Plant Profile

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist to average, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; evaluated alongside other Callicarpa selections in university trials as an alternative to the more commonly grown purple- and white-berried American beautyberry forms.

directions: Sugarloaf Pink is a pink-fruited selection of the native American beautyberry, carrying the same tightly whorled rings of berries along arching stems as the species but in a softer rose-pink shade rather than the vivid magenta-purple of the typical form or the bright pink of the better-known 'Welch's Pink'. The clusters ripen in late summer and persist on the bare stems into winter, offering an extended food source for mockingbirds and other fruit-eating songbirds. Site it at a woodland edge or shade-garden border where its arching, loosely branched habit has room to spread, and prune hard in late winter since the heaviest berry production comes on vigorous new growth. It pairs well with the native purple and white beautyberry forms for a mixed color display along the same planting.
sources: University of Delaware Botanic Gardens — Callicarpa Trial

common_name: Berries and Cream Variegated American Beautyberry

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; the cream-marbled foliage of Berries and Cream shows the most pronounced variegation with some protection from the hottest afternoon sun.

directions: Berries and Cream is a variegated-leaf sport of American beautyberry, its foliage marbled through the center and margins with creamy white against the usual deep green, giving the shrub ornamental interest through the whole growing season rather than only at fall fruiting. Despite the lighter foliage it still produces the species' signature tight whorled clusters of bright purple berries along the stems in late summer and fall, so the plant combines a season-long foliage display with the familiar beautyberry fruit show. First circulated through connoisseur plant programs at native plant collections, it remains a specialty-nursery item rather than a big-box staple. Grow it in well-drained soil with some afternoon shade to keep the variegated leaves from scorching, and prune hard in late winter to encourage the vigorous new growth that carries the heaviest berry set.
sources: J.C. Raulston Arboretum — Connoisseur Plants Program
North Carolina State University Extension — Callicarpa americana Plant Profile

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in moist, organically rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Koehnei is a rare, very slow-growing dwarf selection well suited to small gardens or large containers.

directions: Koehnei is a slow-growing, compact selection of red buckeye that stays considerably smaller than the straight species while still carrying upright panicles of rose-pink flowers in late spring, a softer color than the typical scarlet-red bloom of the wild form. New spring foliage emerges with a bronzed cast before settling to light green, adding an extra season of interest beyond the flower display. Its reduced scale and architectural, miniature-tree habit make it a fitting choice for a shaded foundation planting, container culture, or a small woodland garden where a full-sized buckeye would quickly outgrow the space. Grow in moist, humus-rich soil with some afternoon shade, and expect the same early-summer dormancy and leaf drop as other red buckeye forms during hot, dry stretches; all plant parts are toxic if ingested.

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil tolerant of both acidic and alkaline conditions, in full sun to partial shade; Serenity is a patented clonal selection offered own-root and summer-dug.

directions: Serenity is a clonal selection of native white fringetree chosen for a broader, denser canopy than typical seedling-grown trees, giving a fuller rounded-to-upright silhouette once established. In spring it produces the same airy, cloud-like drifts of drooping white flower panicles that make the species one of the most striking native flowering trees of the eastern United States, with noticeably strong early vigor compared to seed-grown stock. Clear yellow fall foliage adds a second season of interest after the spring bloom fades. Its tolerance of both acidic and alkaline soils makes it more adaptable to urban planting sites than most small native flowering trees, and it performs well as a single-trunk specimen or trained tree-form planting along a partly shaded border or street edge.

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Lagniappe is a patented clonal selection offered own-root through wholesale tree nurseries.

directions: Lagniappe is a clonal selection of native white fringetree named for the Louisiana French term for 'a little something extra,' chosen for foliage that stays darker and more lustrous through the heat of summer than typical seedling-grown trees. It produces the same profuse, drooping clusters of fragrant white flowers in spring that give the species its airy, cloud-like floral display, carried on a round-to-upright canopy similar in scale to other named fringetree selections. The glossy summer foliage holds its color and vigor well into fall, giving the tree a tidier appearance through the growing season than many seed-grown specimens. It suits the same partly shaded woodland-edge and foundation-planting roles as other fringetree cultivars, requiring little maintenance once established beyond occasional removal of crossing interior branches.
